newsitem.title: CUBA: U.S. officials in Cuba investigating July hijack.
newsitem.headline: U.S. officials in Cuba investigating July hijack.

text.p: An FBI agent and a U.S. Justice Department official were in Cuba on Wednesday investigating a hijack in July in which a Cuban forced a commercial plane to fly to the U.S. Naval Base at Guantanamo Bay.

A spokeswoman at the U.S. Interests Section in Havana told Reuters the two were investigating the case but declined to give additional details, saying it was U.S. policy not to comment on investigations in progress.

Cuban Foreign Ministry official Rafael Dausa confirmed the U.S. officials were in Cuba, saying they arrived last weekend and would stay for about a week. He also declined to give details other than to say that they were in Cuba to conduct an investigation.

The hijacker, former Interior Ministry officer Jose Fernandez Pupo, asked for political asylum after forcing a small Cuban passenger plane to fly to the U.S. base, on the southeast tip of Cuba, on July 7. He is in detention in the United States and U.S. authorities have not said what they intend to do with him.

Cuban authorities have repeatedly demanded Fernandez Pupo be returned to Cuba, arguing that failure to do so would breach the terms of a May 1995 bilateral migration accord. Under the agreement, the United States undertook to repatriate Cubans trying to emigrate to the United States by illegal means, whether by sea or by crossing to Guantanamo.

Authorities in Havana have also demanded the return of three other Cubans who hijacked a small taxi plane from Cuba towards Florida on Aug. 16. The plane ditched in the Gulf of Florida and after being rescued the hijackers asked for asylum. The pilot returned home to Cuba.
U.S. authorities have said they plan to try the three Cubans involved in the August incident for air piracy.
Asked about the hijacks, Dausa said Cuba continued to insist the United States should return all four hijackers in order to avoid encouraging similar acts in the future.
